---
name: explain-direction-before-acting
description: Say what you are about to do next, in plain words, before doing it — especially when the user replies "proceed".
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

Before starting work, state the direction in plain words: what happens next,
why, and what it will change. Then do it.

On 2026-09-22 the user explained that when they say "proceed" it is often
because my summary left them unclear on what I was actually going to do next,
so they had no basis to steer. They asked that I explain the direction first,
in plain language, so they can correct course before the work happens rather
than after.

**Why:** a summary of what already happened does not tell them what is coming.
Without that, "proceed" is them deferring rather than agreeing, and the chance
to redirect is lost.

**How to apply:** open with two or three plain sentences on what I am about to
do and what it will produce. No jargon. Then act in the same turn. Keep the
explanation short — it is a heads-up, not a plan document. Applies most when
they reply with a single word like "proceed", which signals they may be
following along rather than directing.

See [[act-on-stated-instructions]]: explaining the direction is not the same as
asking permission again for something already decided.
